title: Only this moment
hook: Marcus: live three thousand years or three, you only lose the present you have (Meditations 2.14)
carry: am I here for the time I've got

segments.voice: Yesterday, qiyas: the grocer's parrot, sure a bald dervish must have spilled oil too. Your line was not the same bald. Today closes the week.

A question people love to ask at dinner parties: if you could live a thousand years, would you? Some say yes, instantly. Think of the books, the places, the grandchildren's grandchildren. Others shudder. Underneath sits a fear many people carry quietly: that life is too short, that it's slipping away day by day, like sand. Marcus Aurelius took that fear seriously, and then did some very clear arithmetic with it. Today, only this moment.
screen: `WOULD YOU LIVE A THOUSAND YEARS?` → `LOSING LIFE LIKE SAND.` → `ONLY THIS MOMENT.`

segments.voice: Meditations 2.14 opens, in George Long's translation: "Though thou shouldst be going to live three thousand years, and as many times ten thousand years, still remember that no man loses any other life than this which he now lives, nor lives any other than this which he now loses." His reasoning: the past is already gone; you can't lose it, because you don't have it. The future isn't here yet; you can't lose that either. The only thing anyone ever has is the present moment, so it's the only thing anyone can lose. And the present, he says, is the same size for everyone. The emperor and the baby, the old woman and the young soldier, all have exactly now. That's why the longest life and the shortest, he concludes, come to the same thing when they end: each person gives up only the moment they're in. Comforting or unsettling? Probably both. But it changes the question. Not how much time will I get, but am I here for the time I've got. Now look back at this week. Rumi's king admitted the proud cures weren't working. His physician from the unseen found the truth by listening to a pulse as a name was spoken. Marcus reminded himself that his time has a limit, and to do each act as if it were the last. The grocer's parrot judged a stranger by its own old story instead of looking at him. A Muslim poet and a Roman emperor don't mean the same thing by any of it. But each, in his own way, kept asking for attention to what is actually here. Only this moment.
screen: `THREE THOUSAND YEARS OR THREE.` · `YOU ONLY HAVE THE PRESENT.` · `THE PRESENT IS THE SAME FOR ALL.` · `NOT HOW LONG, BUT AM I HERE.` · then, large: `ONLY THIS MOMENT.`

segments.voice: Feel your body where it sits, hear whatever sounds are here, notice the light. Let yesterday go for now, and let tomorrow wait; neither is here. Whenever your mind leaves, say inside, only this moment, and come back to this breath, this sound, this weight in the chair.
present moment, the one thing Marcus says anyone can ever have, or lose, however long they live. Today's word.
Your line: am I here for the time I've got. Next week, Rumi's lion, and a very small hare. A full week, done.

howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations often return to 2.14 as a meditation on time, and it is widely quoted in modern Stoic practice alongside mindfulness teaching about attending to the present.
